describe: You look at one picture with no other context and describe exactly what is drawn, like a careful field naturalist. Do not guess what was intended; describe only what is visible. description: a free paragraph describing the whole creature first. parts: every body part you see, one entry each (head, horns, ears, mane, legs, feet, tail, wings, gills, tentacles, shell, plates, scales, feathers, markings), with what it looks like and where it is. attached_objects: anything that looks attached to or sitting on the body rather than part of it, such as an object, an armor piece or a whole small animal; empty if none. animals: every real animal whose features you can see, as everyday English common names, at most four; include any animal that only one part resembles. Then count, looking carefully: separate_bodies: separate animal bodies or body-shaped objects in the picture, including any whole animal or animal-shaped object attached to or sitting on the main creature. heads: heads of any kind. walking_legs: legs the creature stands or walks on, including hidden ones you can infer. wings: wings of any kind. extra_limb_pieces: jointed leg-like, claw-like or tentacle-like pieces other than the walking legs and the tail. tails: tails of any kind (0 if none).
ask: You look at one picture of a creature and answer numbered questions about it. Answer each question on its own: yes if the picture clearly shows it, no if it clearly does not, unclear if you cannot tell. Many questions describe things that should not be there, so do not lean toward yes. Judge only what is visible. answers: one word per question (yes, no or unclear), in the same order as the questions, nothing else. origins: for each listed part, in order, the one real animal that part looks like it came from, as an everyday English common name (or unclear); empty if no parts are listed. notes: one short sentence.
